About This Book

This phonics and spelling workbook belongs to Crystal Heights International School. It was prepared by the school's Phonics Team to build the foundation skills Grade 3 learners need before moving on to Grade 5 and 6.

How to Use This Book

Most lessons cover 7 stages across 7 pages. Lessons that build brand-new sounds skip Word Meaning and run 6 pages instead. A progress bar at the top of every page shows which stages are complete.

📘 Stage 1: Learn
📋 Stage 2: Word List
🗂 Stage 3: Word Sort
✍️ Stage 4: Prove It
📒 Stage 5: Working Space
📖 Stage 6: Word Meaning

Lesson 1: Consonant and Vowel Slide

A consonant is added to the beginning of a vowel to form a new sound. A slide arrow is used to show that the two letters slide together. All vowels have the short sound.

The Slide is a very important step in fluency. Begin by saying the sound /m/, and slide to /a/. The sound produced is /ma/.

Lesson 4: Introduction to Blends

A Blend is two or three consonants standing together, each letter keeping its own sound. Blends can appear at the beginning or end of a single-syllable word. Blends are difficult to pronounce in isolation — slide to a vowel sound right away. An arc is used to identify a blend in a word.

Lesson 5: Digraphs

Digraphs are made up of consonants and are joined by an arc. They differ from blends in that the letters that make up a blend keep their own sounds, but in digraphs the letters together make only one sound.

CH, SH, WH, TH (voiceless), TH (voiced), and TCH make new sounds you can pronounce with a vowel element. PH, GH, KN, CK, and WR are not new sounds, but new spellings for sounds already learned.

Lesson 6: Special Vowel Combinations

A vowel followed by double-L is called a Special Vowel Combination. The letter L becomes part of the vowel sound. Special Vowel Combinations are marked with an X under the vowel and an arc under all three letters.

A vowel followed by _NG or _NK is also called a Special Vowel Combination and is marked the same way.

Lesson 7: Digraph Blends

R can be joined with unvoiced TH. When L, R, or S are added to the digraph CH, it causes CH to change from /ch/ to /k/. L and R can be added to the digraph PH.

The Digraph Blends are SHR, THR, CHL, CHR, SCH, PHL, and PHR. When proving words with Digraph Blends, mark all three letters together.

Lesson 19: Many Jobs of Y

The letter Y says its consonant sound only if it is the first letter in a word. If Y comes anywhere else, it functions as a vowel; apply the Five Phonetic Skills to find its sound.

Skill 1 (one guardian): short I, as in Myth. Skill 2 (two guardians): short I, as in Crypt. Skill 3 (alone at word end): long I, as in Try. Skill 4 (silent E word): long I, as in Type. Skill 5 (adjacent vowel): silent, as in Day.

pages.name: Glossary
pages.subtitle: KEY TERMS
pages.html:
Glossary
TermMeaning
BlendTwo or three consonants said together, keeping each sound (bl, str).
ConsonantAny letter of the alphabet other than a, e, i, o, u.
DecodableA word or passage that can be sounded out using rules already taught.
DigraphTwo letters that make one brand new sound (ch, sh, ph, kn).
Guardian ConsonantA consonant that guards a short vowel and keeps it short.
Long VowelA vowel that says its own name (cake, he, boat).
PhonicsA method of teaching reading that links letters to sounds.
ProveTo mark a word to show which phonetic rule it follows.
Short VowelA vowel with a quick sound (cat, bed, sit, hot, cup).
Silent EAn e at the end of a word that is not said, but makes the vowel before it long.
SuffixA group of letters added to the end of a word (-ing, -ed, -er, -est).
Vowel TeamTwo vowels together that make one sound (ea, ee, oa, ie, oe).
